One step of the case analysis is still open, and it is the step the first case took explicitly. Condition (4.4.17) puts D\mathcal DD inside Dθ\mathcal D_\thetaDθ​ without saying the two are equal, and a subspace of a symmetric domain is symmetric as well, so containment on its own settles nothing. But the operator on a proper subspace cannot be self-adjoint. If D\mathcal DD is strictly inside Dθ\mathcal D_\thetaDθ​, then p^θ\hat p_\thetap^​θ​ extends −iℏ d/dx-\ii\hbar\,\dd/\dd x−iℏd/dx on D\mathcal DD, so (4.4.10) makes the adjoint's domain contain dom⁡(p^θ†)=Dθ\operatorname{dom}(\hat p_\theta^{\dagger})=\mathcal D_\thetadom(p^​θ†​)=Dθ​, which is strictly larger than D\mathcal DD. So D=Dθ\mathcal D=\mathcal D_\thetaD=Dθ​ exactly, and the phases are the whole list.

Since θ\thetaθ and θ+2π\theta+2\piθ+2π give the same condition, the family is a circle. Momentum on a bounded interval is not one observable but a circle of them, and they are genuinely different operators, because their eigenvalues differ. Solving −iℏψ′=pψ-\ii\hbar\psi'=p\psi−iℏψ′=pψ gives ψ=eipx/ℏ\psi=\ee^{\ii px/\hbar}ψ=eipx/ℏ, and the condition in (4.4.17) reads eipL/ℏ=eiθ\ee^{\ii pL/\hbar}=\ee^{\ii\theta}eipL/ℏ=eiθ, so

pn  =  ℏ (θ+2πn)L,n∈Z. p_n \;=\; \frac{\hbar\,(\theta+2\pi n)}{L}, \qquad n\in\mathbb{Z} . pn​=Lℏ(θ+2πn)​,n∈Z. (4.4.18)

A whole ladder of allowed momenta, sliding rigidly as θ\thetaθ turns, and returning to itself after one full turn. Choosing θ\thetaθ is choosing what happens at the wall, and §7 will show the same phenomenon for energy with more room in it.

5.5 · The half-line: the term that cannot be killed

Take (a,b)=(0,∞)(a,b)=(0,\infty)(a,b)=(0,∞), which is the case Chapter 4.2 §4 named twice. The end at infinity is handled by §5.3's argument word for word, so the boundary term of (4.4.13) is one number:

⟨p^u, v⟩−⟨u, p^v⟩  =  − iℏ u(0)‾ v(0). \avg{\hat pu,\,v}-\avg{u,\,\hat pv} \;=\; -\,\ii\hbar\,\overline{u(0)}\,v(0). ⟨p^​u,v⟩−⟨u,p^​v⟩=−iℏu(0)​v(0). (4.4.19)

Ask the same question as before: for which domains does this vanish on every pair? Set u=vu=vu=v in (4.4.19) and the answer arrives at once, because ∣v(0)∣2=0\abs{v(0)}^{2}=0∣v(0)∣2=0 has only one solution. Every vvv in a symmetric domain must satisfy v(0)=0v(0)=0v(0)=0. There is no phase to choose, because there is only one endpoint and a phase relates two.

So the largest symmetric domain available is D0={v:v′∈L2, v(0)=0}\mathcal D_{0}=\{v:v'\in L^{2},\ v(0)=0\}D0​={v:v′∈L2, v(0)=0}, and we can ask whether that one is self-adjoint. Section 5.2 gives its adjoint's domain as every uuu with u′∈L2u'\in L^{2}u′∈L2 and no condition at zero, since (4.4.19) already vanishes once v(0)=0v(0)=0v(0)=0. That is strictly larger: the function u(x)=e−x/au(x)=\ee^{-x/a}u(x)=e−x/a, for any length aaa, has u′∈L2u'\in L^{2}u′∈L2 and u(0)=1u(0)=1u(0)=1, so it sits in the adjoint's domain and not in D0\mathcal D_0D0​. The operator is symmetric and not self-adjoint.

Now put the two paragraphs together, which is the step that makes this different from §5.4. In that section the repair was to enlarge the domain until the two met. Here enlarging is not available: any enlargement contains a function with v(0)≠0v(0)\ne0v(0)=0, and the first paragraph shows that such a domain is not symmetric, so it is not a candidate at all. The domain cannot grow and the adjoint's domain cannot shrink. They never meet.

⚠ The conclusion, which is a fact about nature and not about notation

−iℏ d/dx-\ii\hbar\,\dd/\dd x−iℏd/dx on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) is symmetric and has no self-adjoint extension whatever. By P2 as corrected in §4.2, the momentum of a particle confined to a half-line is not an observable. There is no operator to measure, so there is no spectrum of possible values, no probability distribution over them, and no expectation value beyond the formal integral.

Nothing was quoted to reach that. It is (4.4.13), which is integration by parts, together with the observation that ∣v(0)∣2=0\abs{v(0)}^{2}=0∣v(0)∣2=0 forces v(0)=0v(0)=0v(0)=0.

Where it bites. A radial coordinate runs over [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞), so this is the statement that there is no radial momentum observable, and it is the reason Chapter 4.13 has to argue for the behaviour of the hydrogen wavefunction at the origin rather than assume it. It is also why Chapter 4.7's infinite well cannot be declared to have ψ=0\psi=0ψ=0 at the walls without an argument: that is one choice among the family §7 counts, and the physics of the wall is what selects it.

And notice what did not go wrong. Momentum on a half-line has real expectation values, real would-be eigenvalues, and a perfectly sensible-looking formula. Every check §4.3 listed passes. The failure is invisible until you ask the one question this chapter taught you to ask.

The reason for the asymmetry deserves a sentence, because it is Chapter 0.5's fourth item returning under a different name. On a bounded interval, whatever leaves one end can be made to arrive at the other, and θ\thetaθ records how much phase it picks up on the way. On a half-line there is a place to go and nowhere to come from. That is exactly the shift S^\hat SS^ of (4.4.1): norm-preserving, one-to-one, and not onto. Worked example 3 makes the identification precise by exponentiating p^\hat pp^​ and finding that the flow it generates runs in one direction only.

In plain terms 4.4.5

Everything in this section is one line of calculus done honestly. When you move a derivative from one function to the other inside an integral, a leftover appears at the two ends of the interval. In Part 0 it was always thrown away, with the note that throwing it away is a physical claim. Here it is the only thing being looked at, because it is precisely the obstruction to a momentum operator being a measurable quantity.

On an infinite line the leftover disappears by itself. Anything with finite total probability and a finite spread of momentum has to die away at both ends, so there is nothing to arrange and nothing to choose, and momentum is a perfectly ordinary observable. On a segment the leftover is the difference between the two ends, and it can be cancelled by insisting that whatever leaves one end arrives at the other with a fixed change of phase. The size of that change is a real number, free to be anything, and every value of it gives a different genuine momentum operator with a different ladder of allowed values. The condition at the wall is not bookkeeping. It is a physical input, and the measurable momenta depend on it.

On a half-line the arithmetic gives a different kind of answer. The leftover involves one end only, and the sole way to cancel it is to demand that every state vanish there, which is a demand so strong that the partner operator is left with a larger list of states than the operator itself and no amount of adjustment closes the gap. The conclusion is not a technicality: a particle held on one side of an impenetrable wall has no momentum observable at all. Not one that is hard to compute. One that does not exist.

a natural place to stop  ·  the answers are in hand; what follows is the theorem that counts them

6 · Counting the extensions: deficiency indices

Section 5 produced three answers by hand: a unique operator, a circle of them, and none. This section quotes the theorem that predicts which of those three outcomes occurs, without solving a boundary-value problem, and reduces the prediction to counting the square-integrable solutions of one first-order equation. It has to reproduce §5 exactly three times, and it does.

6.1 · The question, in a form a theorem can answer

Section 3.4 said what the general situation looks like. A symmetric operator sits inside its adjoint, enlarging the operator shrinks the adjoint, and a self-adjoint extension is a place where the two meet. So the size of the gap between dom⁡(A^)\operatorname{dom}(\hat A)dom(A^) and dom⁡(A^†)\operatorname{dom}(\hat A^{\dagger})dom(A^†) is what decides everything, and the useful way to measure that gap is to look at what A^†\hat A^{\dagger}A^† can do that A^\hat AA^ cannot.

The measurement von Neumann found is this. A symmetric operator has real eigenvalues, by §4.3, so it can have no eigenvector with a strictly complex eigenvalue. Its adjoint has a larger domain and is under no such restriction, so it can. Counting the eigenvectors of A^†\hat A^{\dagger}A^† at one complex eigenvalue above the axis and at its mirror image below measures exactly how much room there is between the operator and its adjoint, and that count is what the theorem is stated in terms of.

6.2 · The classification, quoted

⚑ Quoted, not derived — von Neumann's classification of self-adjoint extensions

We use, without proof, the following. Let A^\hat AA^ be symmetric with a dense domain in a Hilbert space. Fix any positive number λ\lambdaλ carrying the units of A^\hat AA^, and define the two deficiency spaces and their dimensions. They take an N\mathcal NN rather than the D\mathcal DD this chapter has been using for domains, because they are not domains of anything: they are the sets of solutions of an eigenvalue equation, sitting inside a domain already fixed.

N±  =  {f∈dom⁡(A^†) : A^†f=± iλf},n±=dim⁡N±. \mathcal{N}_{\pm} \;=\; \big\{f\in\operatorname{dom}(\hat A^{\dagger})\ :\ \hat A^{\dagger}f=\pm\,\ii\lambda f\big\}, \qquad n_{\pm}=\dim\mathcal{N}_{\pm}. N±​={f∈dom(A^†) : A^†f=±iλf},n±​=dimN±​.

The two numbers do not depend on which λ\lambdaλ was chosen. They are the deficiency indices, written (n+,n−)(n_+,n_-)(n+​,n−​), and they settle the question completely.

  • (0,0)(0,0)(0,0). Exactly one self-adjoint operator extends A^\hat AA^.
  • (n,n)(n,n)(n,n) with n≥1n\ge1n≥1. The self-adjoint operators extending A^\hat AA^ correspond one-to-one with the unitary maps of N+\mathcal{N}_{+}N+​ onto N−\mathcal{N}_{-}N−​. That set of maps is U(n)U(n)U(n), and it has n2n^{2}n2 real parameters.
  • n+≠n−n_+\ne n_-n+​=n−​. There are none.

What the mark covers and what it does not. The proof runs through the Cayley transform, which turns a symmetric operator into an isometry and a self-adjoint one into a unitary, so that extending the operator becomes extending an isometry and the count becomes linear algebra on the two leftover spaces. It is about six pages and it is in Reed and Simon's Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics, volume II, and in Rudin. The mark also covers the technical point that the deficiency spaces are read off A^†\hat A^{\dagger}A^† alone, so nothing about A^\hat AA^ beyond symmetry and density enters the count. What the mark does not cover is any of §5, which used none of this.

Why it is computable. The deficiency spaces are read off A^†\hat A^{\dagger}A^†, and for the operators of §5 that domain came out maximal, with no endpoint condition surviving. So finding the deficiency spaces means solving a differential equation with no boundary conditions at all and then asking which solutions are square integrable. For a first-order operator that is one line of calculus.

6.3 · The three cases, counted

Say first which operator is being extended in each case, since the theorem counts the extensions of a given one. On the line it is p^\hat pp^​ on (4.4.7). On the interval it is p^\hat pp^​ on Dmin⁡\mathcal D_{\min}Dmin​, the pinned domain, which is the smallest sensible starting point and the one whose adjoint §5.4 computed. On the half-line it is p^\hat pp^​ on D0\mathcal D_{0}D0​. In all three the adjoint acts by the same formula on the maximal domain, so the calculation is the same one three times over.

Take λ\lambdaλ to be a fixed positive momentum p0p_0p0​, so that the units work. The equation p^†f=±ip0f\hat p^{\dagger}f=\pm\ii p_0 fp^​†f=±ip0​f is −iℏf′=±ip0f-\ii\hbar f'=\pm\ii p_0f−iℏf′=±ip0​f, so f′=∓p0f/ℏf'=\mp p_0f/\hbarf′=∓p0​f/ℏ and

p^†f=+ip0f ⟹ f=e−p0x/ℏ,p^†f=−ip0f ⟹ f=e+p0x/ℏ, \hat p^{\dagger}f=+\ii p_0 f \ \Longrightarrow\ f=\ee^{-p_0x/\hbar}, \qquad \hat p^{\dagger}f=-\ii p_0 f \ \Longrightarrow\ f=\ee^{+p_0x/\hbar}, p^​†f=+ip0​f ⟹ f=e−p0​x/ℏ,p^​†f=−ip0​f ⟹ f=e+p0​x/ℏ, (4.4.20)

each unique up to a constant, since a first-order equation has a one-dimensional solution space. An exponential has its derivative proportional to itself, so being in the domain of p^†\hat p^{\dagger}p^​† at all reduces to the single question of whether the exponential is square-integrable. Hence n±n_\pmn±​ is 111 when the corresponding exponential lies in L2L^{2}L2 of the interval and 000 when it does not, and that is the entire computation. Take the three intervals in the order §5 took them.

  • The line. e−p0x/ℏ\ee^{-p_0x/\hbar}e−p0​x/ℏ blows up as x→−∞x\to-\inftyx→−∞ and e+p0x/ℏ\ee^{+p_0x/\hbar}e+p0​x/ℏ blows up as x→+∞x\to+\inftyx→+∞, so neither is in L2(R)L^{2}(\R)L2(R) and the indices are (0,0)(0,0)(0,0). Exactly one self-adjoint extension. Section 5.3 found exactly one.
  • The interval. Both exponentials are continuous on a bounded interval, so both are in L2[0,L]L^{2}[0,L]L2[0,L], and the indices are (1,1)(1,1)(1,1). The unitary maps between two one-dimensional spaces are multiplication by a phase, so the family is U(1)U(1)U(1), a circle, with 12=11^{2}=112=1 real parameter. Section 5.4 found a circle, parametrised by one phase.
  • The half-line. e−p0x/ℏ\ee^{-p_0x/\hbar}e−p0​x/ℏ decays and is in L2[0,∞)L^{2}[0,\infty)L2[0,∞), while e+p0x/ℏ\ee^{+p_0x/\hbar}e+p0​x/ℏ grows and is not. The indices are (1,0)(1,0)(1,0), they are unequal, and there are no self-adjoint extensions. Section 5.5 found none.

Three cases, three agreements, and the agreement is not a coincidence of arithmetic. Look at the totals. The sum n++n−n_++n_-n+​+n−​ comes out 000, 222 and 111, which is the number of independent pieces of boundary data the interval carries, because each piece is one thing the boundary term of (4.4.13) has to cancel. For a first derivative that data is one number at each finite end, the value of the function there, which is why the totals here also read as a count of finite endpoints. Take the count of data as the rule and the count of endpoints as a coincidence of first order, because §7 has the same two finite ends and gets (2,2)(2,2)(2,2): a second derivative reads a value and a slope at each of them. Self-adjoint extensions exist when the data can be paired off against itself, which needs an even total split evenly, and that is n+=n−n_+=n_-n+​=n−​. The half-line has one datum and no partner for it. What the theorem adds is that this survives into situations where the hand calculation would be much longer, and §7 is the first of those.

In plain terms 4.4.6

The previous section answered a question three times by direct calculation, and got three different kinds of answer: one operator, a circle of operators, and no operator. A theorem exists that predicts which of the three you are about to get, and it does so by a count that takes a single line.

The recipe is this. Take the partner operator, which has the longer list of allowed states, and look for states it sends to themselves multiplied by a purely imaginary number. The original operator can never do this, because it always returns real multiples, so anything the partner manages here is a direct measurement of how much larger the partner is. Count these states above the axis and below it separately, and the pair of counts decides which of the three answers you are going to get. It gets all three right here, which is why it can be trusted in the next section, where the hand calculation would be considerably longer.

a natural place to stop  ·  the first derivative is finished; what follows is the second, with the machinery put to work

7 · The particle in a box has four parameters, not one

Everything so far has been about a first derivative. Energy is a second derivative, and this section runs the whole machine on it. The boundary term acquires a second pair of terms, the deficiency indices come out (2,2)(2,2)(2,2) rather than (1,1)(1,1)(1,1), and the family of self-adjoint Hamiltonians for a particle in a box is therefore a U(2)U(2)U(2): four real parameters, not one. We then take a one-parameter slice of that family, solve it, and find that different members have genuinely different energy levels. That is the point of the section. The boundary condition is not bookkeeping and it is not a choice of convenience. It is physics, and it is measurable.

7.1 · The boundary form for a second derivative

Take H^=−ℏ22m d2dx2\hat H=-\dfrac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\,\dvn{2}{}{x}H^=−2mℏ2​dx2d2​ on L2[0,L]L^{2}[0,L]L2[0,L], which is Chapter 4.2's free Hamiltonian confined to a box. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives across and leaves two boundary terms rather than one:

⟨H^u, v⟩−⟨u, H^v⟩  =  ℏ22m[ u(x)‾ v′(x)−u′(x)‾ v(x) ]0L. \avg{\hat Hu,\,v}-\avg{u,\,\hat Hv} \;=\; \frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Big[\,\overline{u(x)}\,v'(x)-\overline{u'(x)}\,v(x)\,\Big]_{0}^{L} . ⟨H^u,v⟩−⟨u,H^v⟩=2mℏ2​[u(x)​v′(x)−u′(x)​v(x)]0L​. (4.4.21)

The structure is the same as (4.4.13) and the arithmetic is one step longer. Symmetry on a domain is again the demand that the right-hand side of (4.4.21) vanish for every pair drawn from it, but now the data at each end is a pair of numbers, the value and the slope, so there is more to arrange and more ways to arrange it.

7.2 · The count, and the number it produces

Rather than classify by hand, use §6.2, which is exactly the situation it was quoted for. As §6.3 insisted, the theorem counts the extensions of a given operator, so the first job is to say which operator is being extended. It is the one whose domain kills every boundary number there is:

D00  =  {ψ : ψ′′∈L2[0,L],  ψ(0)=ψ(L)=ψ′(0)=ψ′(L)=0}, \mathcal{D}_{00} \;=\; \big\{\psi\ :\ \psi''\in L^{2}[0,L],\ \ \psi(0)=\psi(L)=\psi'(0)=\psi'(L)=0\big\}, D00​={ψ : ψ′′∈L2[0,L],  ψ(0)=ψ(L)=ψ′(0)=ψ′(L)=0}, (4.4.22)

with H^00\hat H_{00}H^00​ the formula −ℏ22md2dx2-\tfrac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\dvn{2}{}{x}−2mℏ2​dx2d2​ on that domain. All four numbers are killed and not two, which is more than §5.4's Dmin⁡\mathcal D_{\min}Dmin​ asked: that domain pinned the two values and left the slopes free. The distinction decides what is being counted. Pinning the values alone, with ψ′′\psi''ψ′′ in L2L^{2}L2, is the Dirichlet domain, and the list below puts Dirichlet at a single point of the family we are about to count, whereas the operator a family is counted from has to be one that every member of the family extends.

Two hypotheses of §6.2 have to be in place before it can be used. H^00\hat H_{00}H^00​ is symmetric, because every term in the bracket of (4.4.21) carries a factor that vanishes at each end. Its domain is dense, by §3.2's chain with one adjustment: replace each straight ramp there by the ramp sin⁡2(πt/2δ)\sin^{2}(\pi t/2\delta)sin2(πt/2δ) across the same width δ\deltaδ, which meets the flat parts on either side with zero slope and has a bounded second derivative, so the approximating functions lie in (4.4.22) and are no further away in L2L^{2}L2 than the straight ones were. The adjoint of H^00\hat H_{00}H^00​ is then §5.2's answer run twice: the formula on the maximal domain, with no endpoint condition surviving, because the test functions that argument uses vanish identically near both ends and so constrain nothing there. So we solve H^00†f=±iE0f\hat H_{00}^{\dagger}f=\pm\ii E_0fH^00†​f=±iE0​f for a fixed positive energy E0E_0E0​, with no boundary conditions imposed:

−ℏ22mf′′  =  ± iE0 f⟺f′′  =  μ±2f,μ±2=∓ 2m iE0ℏ2. -\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}f'' \;=\; \pm\,\ii E_0\,f \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f''\;=\;\mu_{\pm}^{2}f, \qquad \mu_{\pm}^{2}=\mp\,\frac{2m\,\ii E_0}{\hbar^{2}} . −2mℏ2​f′′=±iE0​f⟺f′′=μ±2​f,μ±2​=∓ℏ22miE0​​. (4.4.23)

What matters about (4.4.23) is not the value of μ±\mu_\pmμ±​ but the order of the equation. A second-order linear equation with constant coefficients has a two-dimensional solution space, spanned by eμx\ee^{\mu x}eμx and e−μx\ee^{-\mu x}e−μx, and every one of those solutions is continuous on the bounded interval [0,L][0,L][0,L] and therefore square-integrable on it, whatever complex number μ\muμ happens to be. Both deficiency spaces are two-dimensional and the indices are (2,2)(2,2)(2,2).

That is where §6.3's rule comes good, and the two versions of it are worth reading against each other here. Two finite ends, two pieces of boundary data at each, four pieces in all, split evenly into (2,2)(2,2)(2,2). Counting data gives the right answer and counting endpoints gives two, which is why §6.3 asked you to keep the first version and treat the second as an accident of first order.

Feed that into §6.2 and the answer is a family of self-adjoint Hamiltonians in one-to-one correspondence with the unitary maps of one two-dimensional space onto another, which is U(2)U(2)U(2):

(n+,n−)=(2,2)⟹a U(2) of self-adjoint extensions,dim⁡RU(2)=4. (n_{+},n_{-})=(2,2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{a } U(2)\ \text{of self-adjoint extensions}, \quad \dim_{\R}U(2)=4 . (n+​,n−​)=(2,2)⟹a U(2) of self-adjoint extensions,dimR​U(2)=4. (4.4.24)

The real dimension of U(n)U(n)U(n) is n2n^{2}n2, and §6.2 quoted that along with the theorem. At n=1n=1n=1 you can check it on sight, a 1×11\times11×1 unitary being a phase and nothing else, but n=2n=2n=2 is not visible that way, so here is the count. A 2×22\times22×2 unitary matrix is one whose two columns are orthonormal. The first column is a unit vector in C2\C^{2}C2: four real numbers with one real equation on them, so three real parameters. The second column has to be a unit vector orthogonal to the first, and the vectors orthogonal to a given non-zero vector in C2\C^{2}C2 form a line of one complex dimension, on which the unit vectors differ by a phase. One more real parameter, and three and one make four.

Four real parameters. That is worth stating loudly, because the number one is easy to arrive at and wrong. Momentum on an interval gave a single phase in §5.4, the ladder in (4.4.18) slid rigidly as that phase turned, and it is natural to carry the picture across. Energy is a second derivative, the boundary data at each end is a value and a slope, and the family is four-dimensional. Some familiar conditions and where they sit in it:

  • Dirichlet, ψ(0)=ψ(L)=0\psi(0)=\psi(L)=0ψ(0)=ψ(L)=0, which is the textbook infinite well. One point of U(2)U(2)U(2).
  • Neumann, ψ′(0)=ψ′(L)=0\psi'(0)=\psi'(L)=0ψ′(0)=ψ′(L)=0. A different point.
  • Periodic, ψ(L)=ψ(0)\psi(L)=\psi(0)ψ(L)=ψ(0) and ψ′(L)=ψ′(0)\psi'(L)=\psi'(0)ψ′(L)=ψ′(0), which is a particle on a ring, and antiperiodic, the same with both signs reversed. Two more.
  • The Robin family, ψ′(0)=α ψ(0)\psi'(0)=\alpha\,\psi(0)ψ′(0)=αψ(0) and ψ′(L)=−α ψ(L)\psi'(L)=-\alpha\,\psi(L)ψ′(L)=−αψ(L) with α\alphaα real, a curve through the first two: α=0\alpha=0α=0 is Neumann and the limit of large ∣α∣\abs\alpha∣α∣ is Dirichlet. This is the slice §7.3 works.

Each entry satisfies (4.4.21) directly, and you can check any of them in a line by substituting the two conditions into the bracket. The Robin case is done in full below, including the step from symmetric to self-adjoint, because it is the one whose spectrum we want.

7.3 · The Robin family, worked

Fix a real number α\alphaα with the units of an inverse length and take

dom⁡(H^α)  =  {ψ : ψ′′∈L2[0,L],  ψ′(0)=α ψ(0),  ψ′(L)=−α ψ(L)}. \operatorname{dom}(\hat H_\alpha) \;=\; \big\{\psi\ :\ \psi''\in L^{2}[0,L],\ \ \psi'(0)=\alpha\,\psi(0),\ \ \psi'(L)=-\alpha\,\psi(L)\big\}. dom(H^α​)={ψ : ψ′′∈L2[0,L],  ψ′(0)=αψ(0),  ψ′(L)=−αψ(L)}. (4.4.25)

Check symmetry first. Substitute the two conditions into the bracket of (4.4.21) and look at each end separately. At x=Lx=Lx=L the bracket is u(L)‾ (−αv(L))−(−αu(L))‾ v(L)\overline{u(L)}\,(-\alpha v(L))-\overline{(-\alpha u(L))}\,v(L)u(L)​(−αv(L))−(−αu(L))​v(L), which is −αu(L)‾v(L)+αu(L)‾v(L)=0-\alpha\overline{u(L)}v(L)+\alpha\overline{u(L)}v(L)=0−αu(L)​v(L)+αu(L)​v(L)=0 because α\alphaα is real and comes out of the conjugate unchanged. At x=0x=0x=0 the same cancellation happens with the sign the other way. Each end contributes zero on its own, so H^α\hat H_\alphaH^α​ is symmetric.

Self-adjointness is the same computation read backwards, and it starts from §7.2 rather than from nothing. A function with all four boundary numbers zero satisfies the two Robin conditions, so D00⊆dom⁡(H^α)\mathcal{D}_{00}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\hat H_\alpha)D00​⊆dom(H^α​), and (4.4.10) then puts dom⁡(H^α†)\operatorname{dom}(\hat H_\alpha^{\dagger})dom(H^α†​) inside dom⁡(H^00†)\operatorname{dom}(\hat H_{00}^{\dagger})dom(H^00†​), which §7.2 identified as the maximal domain. So let uuu have u′′∈L2u''\in L^{2}u′′∈L2 and no endpoint condition, and demand that the bracket vanish against every v∈dom⁡(H^α)v\in\operatorname{dom}(\hat H_\alpha)v∈dom(H^α​). Substituting the conditions on vvv collects the bracket into

−(α u(L)‾+u′(L)‾) v(L)  −  (α u(0)‾−u′(0)‾) v(0)  =  0. -\big(\alpha\,\overline{u(L)}+\overline{u'(L)}\big)\,v(L) \;-\; \big(\alpha\,\overline{u(0)}-\overline{u'(0)}\big)\,v(0) \;=\;0 . −(αu(L)​+u′(L)​)v(L)−(αu(0)​−u′(0)​)v(0)=0. (4.4.26)

The two numbers v(0)v(0)v(0) and v(L)v(L)v(L) can be prescribed independently inside the domain, because for any pair of target values there is a cubic polynomial matching those values and the two slopes the conditions then demand, and a cubic has exactly four coefficients to do it with. So both brackets in (4.4.26) vanish separately, and conjugating them returns u′(L)=−αu(L)u'(L)=-\alpha u(L)u′(L)=−αu(L) and u′(0)=αu(0)u'(0)=\alpha u(0)u′(0)=αu(0). Those are the conditions defining (4.4.25), so the adjoint's domain is the domain, and H^α\hat H_\alphaH^α​ is self-adjoint for every real α\alphaα.

7.4 · Different extensions, different spectra

Now solve it, because the whole claim of this section is that the choice is physical, and the way to demonstrate that is to show the choice moving the energy levels. Write E=ℏ2k2/2mE=\hbar^{2}k^{2}/2mE=ℏ2k2/2m for a positive energy, so that ψ′′=−k2ψ\psi''=-k^{2}\psiψ′′=−k2ψ and ψ=Acos⁡kx+Bsin⁡kx\psi=A\cos kx+B\sin kxψ=Acoskx+Bsinkx. The condition at x=0x=0x=0 reads Bk=αABk=\alpha ABk=αA, which is solved by A=kA=kA=k and B=αB=\alphaB=α up to scale. Imposing the condition at x=Lx=Lx=L on that function and collecting terms gives one equation in one unknown:

(α2−k2) sin⁡kL  +  2αk cos⁡kL  =  0⟺tan⁡kL  =  2αkk2−α2. (\alpha^{2}-k^{2})\,\sin kL \;+\; 2\alpha k\,\cos kL \;=\;0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \tan kL \;=\; \frac{2\alpha k}{k^{2}-\alpha^{2}} . (α2−k2)sinkL+2αkcoskL=0⟺tankL=k2−α22αk​. (4.4.27)

That is a transcendental equation and it has no closed-form solution, which is itself informative: the clean n2n^{2}n2 spectrum of the textbook box is a property of one point of the family and not of the formula. Two limits are worth reading off before solving it numerically. At α=0\alpha=0α=0 the equation collapses to sin⁡kL=0\sin kL=0sinkL=0, so k=nπ/Lk=n\pi/Lk=nπ/L and En=n2π2ℏ2/2mL2E_n=n^{2}\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}/2mL^{2}En​=n2π2ℏ2/2mL2, which is the Neumann ladder. It runs from n=0n=0n=0, and the n=0n=0n=0 member is the constant function, which the scaling A=kA=kA=k above discards and which the function Δ(E)\Delta(E)Δ(E) defined below puts back. As ∣α∣→∞\abs\alpha\to\infty∣α∣→∞ the condition ψ′(0)=αψ(0)\psi'(0)=\alpha\psi(0)ψ′(0)=αψ(0) forces ψ(0)→0\psi(0)\to0ψ(0)→0 with the slope finite, so the limit is the Dirichlet ladder, the same numbers with n=0n=0n=0 removed and the lowest level at π2ℏ2/2mL2\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}/2mL^{2}π2ℏ2/2mL2.

Negative energies have to be looked for separately, and they are where the family does something the textbook box never does. Put E=−ℏ2κ2/2mE=-\hbar^{2}\kappa^{2}/2mE=−ℏ2κ2/2m with κ>0\kappa\gt0κ>0, repeat the two steps with hyperbolic functions in place of trigonometric ones, and the condition becomes (α2+κ2)sinh⁡κL+2ακcosh⁡κL=0(\alpha^{2}+\kappa^{2})\sinh\kappa L+2\alpha\kappa\cosh\kappa L=0(α2+κ2)sinhκL+2ακcoshκL=0, which needs α<0\alpha\lt0α<0 to have any solution at all. Both cases are captured by one function of the energy, the characteristic function of this boundary-value problem, which shares its name with Chapter 0.9's characteristic function of a distribution and nothing else. It is obtained by dividing (4.4.27) by kkk and letting kkk be imaginary:

Δ(E)  =  (α2−q) s(q)+2α c(q),q=2mEℏ2, \Delta(E) \;=\; (\alpha^{2}-q)\,s(q)+2\alpha\,c(q), \qquad q=\frac{2mE}{\hbar^{2}}, Δ(E)=(α2−q)s(q)+2αc(q),q=ℏ22mE​, (4.4.28)

where s(q)=sin⁡(q L)/qs(q)=\sin(\sqrt q\,L)/\sqrt qs(q)=sin(q​L)/q​ and c(q)=cos⁡(q L)c(q)=\cos(\sqrt q\,L)c(q)=cos(q​L), both of which are power series in qqq with infinite radius of convergence and are therefore perfectly well defined for qqq negative, where they become sinh⁡\sinhsinh and cosh⁡\coshcosh. The energies are the zeros of Δ\DeltaΔ, and because Δ\DeltaΔ depends smoothly on α\alphaα as well as on EEE, the levels slide continuously as α\alphaα is turned.

One value of Δ\DeltaΔ can be read without any computation and it predicts the whole qualitative story. At q=0q=0q=0 we have s=Ls=Ls=L and c=1c=1c=1, so

Δ(0)  =  α2L+2α  =  α (αL+2), \Delta(0) \;=\; \alpha^{2}L+2\alpha \;=\; \alpha\,(\alpha L+2), Δ(0)=α2L+2α=α(αL+2), (4.4.29)

which vanishes at α=0\alpha=0α=0 and at α=−2/L\alpha=-2/Lα=−2/L and nowhere else. Those are the only two settings at which a level sits exactly at zero energy, so they are the only two at which a level can pass from one side of zero to the other. Solving the equation confirms that nothing else happens: below zero there are no states for α>0\alpha\gt0α>0, one state for −2/L<α<0-2/L\lt\alpha\lt0−2/L<α<0, and two for α<−2/L\alpha\lt-2/Lα<−2/L. A negative α\alphaα makes each wall attractive, and the two thresholds in (4.4.29) are where the first and then the second state bound to a wall drops below the bottom of the positive ladder.

Solving (4.4.28) by Newton's method gives the numbers. Energies are in units of ℏ2/2mL2\hbar^{2}/2mL^{2}ℏ2/2mL2, and the last column is the Dirichlet limit for comparison.

Read the middle column first. At α=0\alpha=0α=0 the roots of (4.4.28) come out at n2π2n^{2}\pi^{2}n2π2 to every digit printed, which is the check that the numerical method is solving the equation we wrote down rather than a neighbour of it. Then read across. The three columns are three different sets of numbers. Same particle, same mass, same box, same formula for the energy, and three different spectra, because three different self-adjoint operators were selected out of the same U(2)U(2)U(2).

The physical reading is the point of the whole chapter and it is worth stating without hedging. The formula −ℏ2ψ′′/2m-\hbar^{2}\psi''/2m−ℏ2ψ′′/2m does not determine a Hamiltonian for a particle in a box. It determines a four-parameter family of them, all self-adjoint, all legitimate observables, with different energy levels. Choosing among them is not a mathematical formality performed before the physics starts. It is the physics of what the wall is made of, and any experiment that measures the levels is measuring which member of the family the wall implements.

In plain terms 4.4.7

Energy involves a second derivative rather than a first, so at each wall there are two numbers to worry about instead of one: the value of the wavefunction and its slope. Running the counting recipe gives two independent directions of freedom at each end rather than one, and the family of legitimate energy operators for a particle in a box turns out to have four adjustable real numbers in it. Four, not one. The single knob belonged to momentum, where each wall carries one number, and it does not carry over.

Every boundary condition anyone writes down for a box is one point of that family. The textbook condition that the wavefunction vanishes at both walls is one point. Demanding instead that the slope vanish is another. Gluing the two ends together into a ring is a third. A wall that is neither perfectly hard nor perfectly soft sits somewhere in between, on a curve through the family that can be solved and plotted.

And the levels move. Turning the knob slides every energy continuously, and past a certain setting a level drops below zero altogether and becomes a state stuck to the wall rather than rattling around inside. Same particle, same box, same formula, different numbers on the spectrometer. That is the sense in which the condition at the boundary is not bookkeeping. It is a physical property of the wall, it is one of the four numbers, and it is measurable.

8 · Worked examples

Worked example 1 — position, where the domain is forced and there is nothing to choose

On L2(R)L^{2}(\R)L2(R) let x^\hat xx^ be multiplication by xxx. (a) Show that x^\hat xx^ is unbounded. (b) Write down the largest domain on which the formula lands back in the space, and show it is dense. (c) Show that x^\hat xx^ is symmetric on it. (d) Show that dom⁡(x^†)\operatorname{dom}(\hat x^{\dagger})dom(x^†) is the same set, so x^\hat xx^ is self-adjoint. (e) Say why no analogue of §5.4's circle appears.

(a) Take ψn\psi_nψn​ to be 1[n,n+1]\mathbf 1_{[n,n+1]}1[n,n+1]​, which has ∥ψn∥=1\norm{\psi_n}=1∥ψn​∥=1. Then x^ψn\hat x\psi_nx^ψn​ is xxx on [n,n+1][n,n+1][n,n+1] and zero elsewhere, so ∥x^ψn∥2=∫nn+1x2dx≥n2\norm{\hat x\psi_n}^{2}=\int_n^{n+1}x^{2}\dd x\ge n^{2}∥x^ψn​∥2=∫nn+1​x2dx≥n2 and the ratio in (4.4.2) is at least nnn. The supremum is infinite. As with momentum, the reason is physical: there is no largest position.

(b) The largest domain is dom⁡(x^)={ψ∈L2:xψ∈L2}\operatorname{dom}(\hat x)=\{\psi\in L^{2}:x\psi\in L^{2}\}dom(x^)={ψ∈L2:xψ∈L2}. It is dense because the truncations ψ1[−R,R]\psi\mathbf 1_{[-R,R]}ψ1[−R,R]​ all lie in it, since xxx is bounded by RRR there, and ∥ψ−ψ1[−R,R]∥→0\norm{\psi-\psi\mathbf 1_{[-R,R]}}\to0​ψ−ψ1[−R,R]​​→0 as R→∞R\to\inftyR→∞ by dominated convergence with ∣ψ∣2\abs\psi^{2}∣ψ∣2 as the dominating function, which is Chapter 4.3 §4.3.

(c) For u,vu,vu,v in the domain, ⟨x^u,v⟩=∫xu‾ v=∫x u‾ v\avg{\hat xu,v}=\int\overline{xu}\,v=\int x\,\overline u\,v⟨x^u,v⟩=∫xuv=∫xuv since xxx is real, and that is ⟨u,x^v⟩\avg{u,\hat xv}⟨u,x^v⟩. The integrals converge because xuxuxu and vvv are both in L2L^{2}L2. There is no integration by parts and therefore no boundary term.

(d) Let u∈dom⁡(x^†)u\in\operatorname{dom}(\hat x^{\dagger})u∈dom(x^†) with witness www, so ∫w‾v=∫u‾ xv\int\overline w v=\int\overline u\,xv∫wv=∫uxv for every vvv in the domain. Taking vvv supported in a bounded interval, this says w=xuw=xuw=xu almost everywhere on that interval, and letting the interval grow gives w=xuw=xuw=xu on the line. Since w∈L2w\in L^{2}w∈L2 by definition of the adjoint's domain, xu∈L2xu\in L^{2}xu∈L2 and u∈dom⁡(x^)u\in\operatorname{dom}(\hat x)u∈dom(x^). So the two domains coincide.

(e) Because there is no boundary term to cancel. The whole family of §5.4 came from (4.4.13), which exists because integration by parts moves a derivative and leaves a remainder at the ends. Multiplication moves nothing. Running §6.2 confirms it: solving xf=±ix0fxf=\pm\ii x_0fxf=±ix0​f gives (x∓ix0)f=0(x\mp\ii x_0)f=0(x∓ix0​)f=0, so fff vanishes wherever x≠±ix0x\ne\pm\ii x_0x=±ix0​, which is everywhere on the real line, and fff is the zero vector. The indices are (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) and the extension is unique. Position and momentum on the line are alike in being forced and unbounded, and unlike in where the difficulty sits: for x^\hat xx^ the domain is the only issue, and for p^\hat pp^​ the domain is the beginning of the issue.

Worked example 2 — squaring a self-adjoint momentum does not give every box Hamiltonian

On [0,L][0,L][0,L] take p^θ\hat p_\thetap^​θ​ from §5.4. (a) Write down the domain of p^θ2\hat p_\theta^{2}p^​θ2​. (b) Find its spectrum. (c) Show that the Dirichlet Hamiltonian is not p^θ2\hat p_\theta^{2}p^​θ2​ for any θ\thetaθ. (d) Say what this means about the sentence "kinetic energy is p2/2mp^{2}/2mp2/2m".

(a) Applying an operator twice requires the intermediate vector to be in the domain again, so dom⁡(p^θ2)={ψ:ψ∈Dθ and p^θψ∈Dθ}\operatorname{dom}(\hat p_\theta^{2})=\{\psi:\psi\in\mathcal D_\theta \text{ and } \hat p_\theta\psi\in\mathcal D_\theta\}dom(p^​θ2​)={ψ:ψ∈Dθ​ and p^​θ​ψ∈Dθ​}. Since p^θψ\hat p_\theta\psip^​θ​ψ is ψ′\psi'ψ′ up to a constant, this is

ψ′′∈L2,ψ(L)=eiθψ(0),ψ′(L)=eiθψ′(0). \psi''\in L^{2}, \qquad \psi(L)=\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi(0), \qquad \psi'(L)=\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi'(0). ψ′′∈L2,ψ(L)=eiθψ(0),ψ′(L)=eiθψ′(0).

Two conditions, which is the right number for a point of the U(2)U(2)U(2) of §7.2, and the family p^θ2/2m\hat p_\theta^{2}/2mp^​θ2​/2m is a one-parameter curve inside that four-parameter family.

(b) The eigenvalues are the squares of those in (4.4.18), divided by 2m2m2m:

En  =  pn22m  =  ℏ2(θ+2πn)22mL2,n∈Z. E_n \;=\; \frac{p_n^{2}}{2m} \;=\; \frac{\hbar^{2}(\theta+2\pi n)^{2}}{2mL^{2}}, \qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}. En​=2mpn2​​=2mL2ℏ2(θ+2πn)2​,n∈Z.

At θ=0\theta=0θ=0 this is the ring, with a ground state at zero energy and every level above it doubly degenerate, since nnn and −n-n−n give the same energy.

(c) Suppose the Dirichlet operator, whose domain requires ψ(0)=ψ(L)=0\psi(0)=\psi(L)=0ψ(0)=ψ(L)=0 and nothing about the slopes, equalled p^θ2\hat p_\theta^{2}p^​θ2​ for some θ\thetaθ. Two operators are equal only when their domains agree, so compare the domains. The function ψ(x)=sin⁡(πx/L)\psi(x)=\sin(\pi x/L)ψ(x)=sin(πx/L) has ψ(0)=ψ(L)=0\psi(0)=\psi(L)=0ψ(0)=ψ(L)=0, so it is in the Dirichlet domain. Its derivative is (π/L)cos⁡(πx/L)(\pi/L)\cos(\pi x/L)(π/L)cos(πx/L), giving ψ′(0)=π/L\psi'(0)=\pi/Lψ′(0)=π/L and ψ′(L)=−π/L\psi'(L)=-\pi/Lψ′(L)=−π/L, so ψ′(L)=eiθψ′(0)\psi'(L)=\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi'(0)ψ′(L)=eiθψ′(0) would force eiθ=−1\ee^{\ii\theta}=-1eiθ=−1 and hence θ=π\theta=\piθ=π. But then the first condition demands ψ(L)=−ψ(0)\psi(L)=-\psi(0)ψ(L)=−ψ(0), and both are zero, which is consistent, so test a second function. Take ϕ(x)=sin⁡(2πx/L)\phi(x)=\sin(2\pi x/L)ϕ(x)=sin(2πx/L), also Dirichlet, with ϕ′(0)=ϕ′(L)=2π/L\phi'(0)=\phi'(L)=2\pi/Lϕ′(0)=ϕ′(L)=2π/L, which needs eiθ=+1\ee^{\ii\theta}=+1eiθ=+1. No single θ\thetaθ serves both, so the Dirichlet domain is not dom⁡(p^θ2)\operatorname{dom}(\hat p_\theta^{2})dom(p^​θ2​) for any θ\thetaθ. The spectra confirm it independently. The lowest level of p^θ2/2m\hat p_\theta^{2}/2mp^​θ2​/2m is ℏ2θ∗2/2mL2\hbar^{2}\theta_{*}^{2}/2mL^{2}ℏ2θ∗2​/2mL2 with θ∗=min⁡n∣θ+2πn∣\theta_{*}=\min_{n}\abs{\theta+2\pi n}θ∗​=minn​∣θ+2πn∣, which never exceeds π\piπ, while Dirichlet's lowest is π2ℏ2/2mL2\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}/2mL^{2}π2ℏ2/2mL2. The two agree only at θ=π\theta=\piθ=π, and there the level is doubly degenerate, from n=0n=0n=0 and n=−1n=-1n=−1, while every Dirichlet level is simple.

(d) The sentence survives as a statement about formulae and fails as a statement about operators. On the line it is exact, because §5.3 gives a unique p^\hat pp^​ and squaring it gives the unique free Hamiltonian. In a box it is not, and part (c) is the whole reason. Momentum observables on [0,L][0,L][0,L] are not in short supply, but §5.4 showed that every one of them is some p^θ\hat p_\thetap^​θ​, and part (a) showed that squaring one drags the slope condition ψ′(L)=eiθψ′(0)\psi'(L)=\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi'(0)ψ′(L)=eiθψ′(0) along with it. The Dirichlet domain imposes nothing on the slopes, and part (c) turned that difference into two of its own members, sin⁡(πx/L)\sin(\pi x/L)sin(πx/L) and sin⁡(2πx/L)\sin(2\pi x/L)sin(2πx/L), which demand eiθ=−1\ee^{\ii\theta}=-1eiθ=−1 and eiθ=+1\ee^{\ii\theta}=+1eiθ=+1 of the same θ\thetaθ. So the textbook infinite well has a Hamiltonian that is not the square of any momentum observable, and not for want of momentum observables to square. This is worth carrying into Chapter 4.7. The infinite well is not a free particle with a restriction bolted on. It is a different operator, chosen from a family, and the choice is what the walls are.

Worked example 3 — the half-line flow that runs one way, and Chapter 0.5's fourth item

On L2(R)L^{2}(\R)L2(R), Chapter 4.2 §7 writes the flow generated by an observable as e−iG^a/ℏ\ee^{-\ii\hat Ga/\hbar}e−iG^a/ℏ. (a) Show that the flow generated by p^\hat pp^​ on the line is translation. (b) Ask the same question on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) with the domain D0\mathcal D_0D0​ of §5.5, and say what happens for each sign of aaa. (c) Identify the resulting family with (4.4.1). (d) Say how this shows up in the deficiency indices.

(a) Expand e−ip^a/ℏψ\ee^{-\ii\hat pa/\hbar}\psie−ip^​a/ℏψ formally, using p^=−iℏddx\hat p=-\ii\hbar\dv{}{x}p^​=−iℏdxd​:

e−ip^a/ℏψ  =  ∑n≥01n!(−a ddx)nψ  =  ∑n≥0(−a)nn! ψ(n)(x)  =  ψ(x−a), \ee^{-\ii\hat pa/\hbar}\psi \;=\; \sum_{n\ge0}\frac{1}{n!}\left(-a\,\dv{}{x}\right)^{n}\psi \;=\; \sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-a)^{n}}{n!}\,\psi^{(n)}(x) \;=\; \psi(x-a), e−ip^​a/ℏψ=n≥0∑​n!1​(−adxd​)nψ=n≥0∑​n!(−a)n​ψ(n)(x)=ψ(x−a),

which is the Taylor series of ψ\psiψ about xxx, convergent for analytic ψ\psiψ and extending to all of L2L^{2}L2 by continuity since each map ψ↦ψ(⋅−a)\psi\mapsto\psi(\cdot-a)ψ↦ψ(⋅−a) preserves the norm. So p^\hat pp^​ generates translation by aaa, in either direction, and each translation is unitary. That is the content of (0,0)(0,0)(0,0): a full group of motions, invertible, with a self-adjoint generator.

(b) On [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) the map ψ(x)↦ψ(x−a)\psi(x)\mapsto\psi(x-a)ψ(x)↦ψ(x−a) makes sense as a map into L2[0,∞)L^{2}[0,\infty)L2[0,∞) only for a≥0a\ge0a≥0. It slides the function to the right, and the vacated interval [0,a)[0,a)[0,a) is filled with zeros, which joins on continuously precisely because every member of D0\mathcal D_0D0​ vanishes at the origin. For a<0a\lt0a<0 the recipe would need values of ψ\psiψ at negative xxx, and there are none. So there is a flow forwards and no flow backwards.

(c) The forward maps preserve the norm exactly, since sliding does not change ∫∣ψ∣2\int\abs\psi^{2}∫∣ψ∣2, and they are one-to-one, since sliding back recovers the function wherever it was defined. They are not onto: nothing in the image is non-zero on [0,a)[0,a)[0,a). That is exactly (4.4.1) with a continuous parameter in place of a discrete one, and it is Chapter 0.5's "the claim that an injective map is surjective" failing in the flesh. Composition adds the parameters, so the family is a semigroup rather than a group: it has an associative law and no inverses.

(d) A self-adjoint generator would give a two-sided flow, by Chapter 4.5 §9's Stone's theorem, and §5.5 showed there is no self-adjoint generator here. The deficiency indices (1,0)(1,0)(1,0) of §6.3 are the arithmetic of exactly that one-sidedness: one square-integrable solution at +ip0+\ii p_0+ip0​ and none at −ip0-\ii p_0−ip0​, because the exponential that decays at +∞+\infty+∞ has no partner decaying at a left end that does not exist. The three descriptions are one fact: a boundary term that cannot be cancelled, an index pair that cannot be balanced, and a motion that cannot be run backwards.

9 · Your turn

Problem 1 — the domain is not everything, exhibited

(a) Show that 1[0,1]\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}1[0,1]​ is in L2(R)L^{2}(\R)L2(R) and not in dom⁡(p^)\operatorname{dom}(\hat p)dom(p^​). (b) Show that ψ(x)=e−∣x∣\psi(x)=\ee^{-\abs x}ψ(x)=e−∣x∣ is in the domain, and compute p^ψ\hat p\psip^​ψ. (c) Show that dom⁡(p^)\operatorname{dom}(\hat p)dom(p^​) is not closed as a subset of L2L^{2}L2, by exhibiting a sequence in it converging to the function of part (a). (d) Explain why (c) is required by §2.3 rather than merely permitted by it.

Solution

(a) ∫∣1[0,1]∣2=1\int\abs{\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}}^{2}=1∫​1[0,1]​​2=1, so it is in L2L^{2}L2. For membership of the domain it would have to be the integral of some function, and no integral has a jump: if F(x)=∫cxgF(x)=\int_{c}^{x}gF(x)=∫cx​g with ggg locally integrable, then ∣F(x)−F(y)∣≤∫yx∣g∣→0\abs{F(x)-F(y)}\le\int_y^{x}\abs g\to0∣F(x)−F(y)∣≤∫yx​∣g∣→0 as y→xy\to xy→x, so FFF is continuous. The indicator is not continuous at 000 or at 111.

(b) On each half-line e−∣x∣\ee^{-\abs x}e−∣x∣ is smooth, and at the origin it is continuous with a corner. It is the integral of g(x)=−sgn(x)e−∣x∣g(x)=-\mathrm{sgn}(x)\ee^{-\abs x}g(x)=−sgn(x)e−∣x∣, which one checks by evaluating ∫0xg\int_0^{x}g∫0x​g separately for x>0x\gt0x>0 and x<0x\lt0x<0. That ggg is in L2L^{2}L2, with ∥g∥2=∫e−2∣x∣=1\norm g^{2}=\int\ee^{-2\abs x}=1∥g∥2=∫e−2∣x∣=1. So ψ\psiψ is in the domain and p^ψ=iℏ sgn(x)e−∣x∣\hat p\psi=\ii\hbar\,\mathrm{sgn}(x)\ee^{-\abs x}p^​ψ=iℏsgn(x)e−∣x∣. A corner is allowed; a jump is not.

(c) Let ψn\psi_nψn​ be continuous, zero outside [−1/n,1+1/n][-1/n,1+1/n][−1/n,1+1/n], equal to 111 on [0,1][0,1][0,1], and linear on the two ramps of width 1/n1/n1/n. Each is in the domain, being piecewise linear and continuous with a step-function derivative in L2L^{2}L2. The difference from 1[0,1]\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}1[0,1]​ is supported on the two ramps and bounded by 111 there, so ∥ψn−1[0,1]∥2≤2/n→0\norm{\psi_n-\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}}^{2}\le2/n\to0​ψn​−1[0,1]​​2≤2/n→0. The limit is not in the domain by (a), so the domain is not closed.

(d) Suppose the domain were closed. Being dense by §3.2, it would then be all of L2L^{2}L2, and p^\hat pp^​ would be a symmetric operator defined on the whole space. Hellinger–Toeplitz would make it bounded, contradicting §2.2. So the domain of any unbounded symmetric operator is necessarily dense and not closed, which is an uncomfortable combination and is the price of the subject. Notice also the sizes in (c). The ramp derivatives have ∥ψn′∥2=2n\norm{\psi_n'}^{2}=2n∥ψn′​∥2=2n, so the inputs converge while the images run away, which is §2.1's discontinuity happening in front of you.

Problem 2 — the adjoint of an extension

(a) Prove (4.4.10) from (4.4.9) directly. (b) Deduce that if A^\hat AA^ is symmetric and B^\hat BB^ is a symmetric extension of it, then dom⁡(A^)⊆dom⁡(B^)⊆dom⁡(B^†)⊆dom⁡(A^†)\operatorname{dom}(\hat A)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\hat B)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\hat B^{\dagger})\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\hat A^{\dagger})dom(A^)⊆dom(B^)⊆dom(B^†)⊆dom(A^†). (c) Conclude that every self-adjoint extension of a symmetric A^\hat AA^ has a domain lying between dom⁡(A^)\operatorname{dom}(\hat A)dom(A^) and dom⁡(A^†)\operatorname{dom}(\hat A^{\dagger})dom(A^†). (d) Use (c) to give a second proof that momentum on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) has no self-adjoint extension, using only the two domains computed in §5.5.

Solution

(a) Let u∈dom⁡(B^†)u\in\operatorname{dom}(\hat B^{\dagger})u∈dom(B^†), so there is www with ⟨w,v⟩=⟨u,B^v⟩\avg{w,v}=\avg{u,\hat Bv}⟨w,v⟩=⟨u,B^v⟩ for every v∈dom⁡(B^)v\in\operatorname{dom}(\hat B)v∈dom(B^). Every v∈dom⁡(A^)v\in\operatorname{dom}(\hat A)v∈dom(A^) is such a vvv, and B^v=A^v\hat Bv=\hat AvB^v=A^v there, so the same www witnesses u∈dom⁡(A^†)u\in\operatorname{dom}(\hat A^{\dagger})u∈dom(A^†). The containment is that one substitution.

(b) The first containment is the hypothesis. The second is symmetry of B^\hat BB^ in the form (4.4.12). The third is part (a).

(c) A self-adjoint extension B^\hat BB^ is in particular a symmetric extension, and it has dom⁡(B^)=dom⁡(B^†)\operatorname{dom}(\hat B)=\operatorname{dom}(\hat B^{\dagger})dom(B^)=dom(B^†), so the chain in (b) puts that common domain between the two ends. This is the precise form of §3.4's picture: the search for a self-adjoint extension is a search inside a fixed interval of subspaces, which is why the answer is a finite-dimensional family rather than an open-ended construction.

(d) Section 5.5 computed dom⁡(p^)={v(0)=0}\operatorname{dom}(\hat p)=\{v(0)=0\}dom(p^​)={v(0)=0} and dom⁡(p^†)={\operatorname{dom}(\hat p^{\dagger})=\{dom(p^​†)={no condition}\}}. Any self-adjoint extension has a domain D\mathcal DD with {v(0)=0}⊆D⊆{\{v(0)=0\}\subseteq\mathcal D\subseteq\{{v(0)=0}⊆D⊆{no condition}\}} and D\mathcal DD symmetric. If D\mathcal DD is strictly larger than {v(0)=0}\{v(0)=0\}{v(0)=0} it contains some vvv with v(0)≠0v(0)\ne0v(0)=0, and then (4.4.19) with u=vu=vu=v is non-zero, so D\mathcal DD is not symmetric. So D={v(0)=0}\mathcal D=\{v(0)=0\}D={v(0)=0}, which is not self-adjoint. No candidate survives.

Problem 3 — the circle of momenta, and what turning it does

(a) For p^θ\hat p_\thetap^​θ​ on [0,L][0,L][0,L], verify that the eigenfunctions ψn(x)=L−1/2ei(θ+2πn)x/L\psi_n(x)=L^{-1/2}\ee^{\ii(\theta+2\pi n)x/L}ψn​(x)=L−1/2ei(θ+2πn)x/L are normalised and orthogonal. (b) Show that U^ψ=eiθx/Lψ\hat U\psi=\ee^{\ii\theta x/L}\psiU^ψ=eiθx/Lψ is unitary on L2[0,L]L^{2}[0,L]L2[0,L] and maps the periodic domain Dθ=0\mathcal D_{\theta=0}Dθ=0​ of §5.4 onto Dθ\mathcal D_\thetaDθ​. (c) Compute U^†p^θU^\hat U^{\dagger}\hat p_\theta\hat UU^†p^​θ​U^ and read off the relation between the spectra of p^θ\hat p_\thetap^​θ​ and p^0\hat p_0p^​0​. (d) Two operators related as in (c) are unitarily equivalent. Explain why they are nevertheless different observables, and give the experimental statement that distinguishes them.

Solution

(a) ∣ψn∣2=1/L\abs{\psi_n}^{2}=1/L∣ψn​∣2=1/L, so ∫0L∣ψn∣2=1\int_0^{L}\abs{\psi_n}^{2}=1∫0L​∣ψn​∣2=1. For m≠nm\ne nm=n, ⟨ψm,ψn⟩=L−1∫0Le2πi(n−m)x/Ldx=0\avg{\psi_m,\psi_n}=L^{-1}\int_0^{L}\ee^{2\pi\ii(n-m)x/L}\dd x=0⟨ψm​,ψn​⟩=L−1∫0L​e2πi(n−m)x/Ldx=0, the integrand being a full number of periods. Each satisfies ψn(L)=eiθψn(0)\psi_n(L)=\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi_n(0)ψn​(L)=eiθψn​(0) since e2πin=1\ee^{2\pi\ii n}=1e2πin=1.

(b) Multiplication by a function of modulus one preserves ∣ψ∣\abs\psi∣ψ∣ pointwise, hence the norm, and it is invertible by multiplication by the conjugate, so it is unitary. If ψ∈Dθ=0\psi\in\mathcal D_{\theta=0}ψ∈Dθ=0​, meaning ψ(L)=ψ(0)\psi(L)=\psi(0)ψ(L)=ψ(0), then (U^ψ)(L)=eiθψ(L)(\hat U\psi)(L)=\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi(L)(U^ψ)(L)=eiθψ(L) and (U^ψ)(0)=ψ(0)(\hat U\psi)(0)=\psi(0)(U^ψ)(0)=ψ(0), so (U^ψ)(L)=eiθ(U^ψ)(0)(\hat U\psi)(L)=\ee^{\ii\theta}(\hat U\psi)(0)(U^ψ)(L)=eiθ(U^ψ)(0). The map is onto Dθ\mathcal D_\thetaDθ​ because U^†\hat U^{\dagger}U^† reverses it.

(c) By the product rule, p^(eiθx/Lψ)=eiθx/L(p^ψ+ℏθLψ)\hat p(\ee^{\ii\theta x/L}\psi)=\ee^{\ii\theta x/L}\big(\hat p\psi+\tfrac{\hbar\theta}{L}\psi\big)p^​(eiθx/Lψ)=eiθx/L(p^​ψ+Lℏθ​ψ), so U^†p^θU^=p^0+ℏθ/L\hat U^{\dagger}\hat p_\theta\hat U=\hat p_0+\hbar\theta/LU^†p^​θ​U^=p^​0​+ℏθ/L. The spectrum of p^θ\hat p_\thetap^​θ​ is the spectrum of p^0\hat p_0p^​0​ shifted by ℏθ/L\hbar\theta/Lℏθ/L, which is (4.4.18) read again.

(d) Unitary equivalence says the two operators have the same abstract structure, not that they are the same observable of the same system. The measured quantity is momentum in both cases, the states are functions on the same interval, and the sets of possible readings differ by ℏθ/L\hbar\theta/Lℏθ/L, which is a number an experiment reports. The equivalence relabels the states by multiplying them by a position-dependent phase, and the physical statement is that this is not a relabelling one is free to perform, because it moves the very observable at issue. Position it leaves untouched. Both U^\hat UU^ and x^\hat xx^ are multiplication by a function, so they commute exactly, and ∣U^ψ∣2=∣ψ∣2\abs{\hat U\psi}^{2}=\abs{\psi}^{2}​U^ψ​2=∣ψ∣2 at every point, which means the relabelled state says precisely what the original said about where the particle is. Momentum is what moves, and part (c) is the computation: conjugating by U^\hat UU^ turns p^θ\hat p_\thetap^​θ​ into p^0+ℏθ/L\hat p_0+\hbar\theta/Lp^​0​+ℏθ/L, so the relabelling shifts every momentum reading by ℏθ/L\hbar\theta/Lℏθ/L. Two boxes with different θ\thetaθ are told apart by measuring momentum in each and comparing the ladders.

The condition at 000 gives Bκ=αAB\kappa=\alpha ABκ=αA, so take A=κA=\kappaA=κ, B=αB=\alphaB=α. Imposing ψ′(L)=−αψ(L)\psi'(L)=-\alpha\psi(L)ψ′(L)=−αψ(L) and collecting gives the stated identity. For α>0\alpha\gt0α>0 every term is positive when κ>0\kappa\gt0κ>0, so the sum cannot vanish. (d) With L=1L=1L=1 and α=−1\alpha=-1α=−1 the condition of (b) is f(κ)=(1+κ2)sinh⁡κ−2κcosh⁡κ=0f(\kappa)=(1+\kappa^{2})\sinh\kappa-2\kappa\cosh\kappa=0f(κ)=(1+κ2)sinhκ−2κcoshκ=0. For small κ\kappaκ, expanding gives f≈−κf\approx-\kappaf≈−κ, so f<0f\lt0f<0 near zero. Problem 5 — where the four parameters are, and what they are not

(a) Count the real parameters in the boundary data of a box, and explain why a self-adjoint Hamiltonian corresponds to two complex conditions rather than one or three. (b) Verify directly from (4.4.21) that the periodic and antiperiodic conditions are symmetric, and that a mixed pair, ψ(L)=ψ(0)\psi(L)=\psi(0)ψ(L)=ψ(0) with ψ′(L)=−ψ′(0)\psi'(L)=-\psi'(0)ψ′(L)=−ψ′(0), is not. (c) The Robin slice of §7.3 uses the same α\alphaα at both ends. Show that allowing different values α0\alpha_0α0​ and αL\alpha_LαL​ still gives a self-adjoint operator, and say how many of the four parameters that family covers. (d) A student says that since all four parameters give self-adjoint operators, and self-adjointness is the whole of P2, the choice among them cannot matter. Say precisely what is wrong.

Solution

(a) The boundary data is (ψ(0),ψ(L),ψ′(0),ψ′(L))\big(\psi(0),\psi(L),\psi'(0),\psi'(L)\big)(ψ(0),ψ(L),ψ′(0),ψ′(L)), four complex numbers, so eight real ones. A domain is cut out of that data by complex linear conditions, and how many of them there must be is forced from both sides. One condition would leave the boundary term of (4.4.21) non-zero on some pair, so the operator would not be symmetric; three would leave the domain too small, so the adjoint's domain would be strictly larger by (4.4.10) and the operator symmetric but not self-adjoint. Two is the only count that can balance.

(b) With ψ(L)=ψ(0)\psi(L)=\psi(0)ψ(L)=ψ(0) and ψ′(L)=ψ′(0)\psi'(L)=\psi'(0)ψ′(L)=ψ′(0) for both uuu and vvv, the bracket at LLL equals the bracket at 000 term by term, so the difference is zero. With both signs reversed, each factor in each product changes sign, so each product is unchanged and the difference is again zero. For the mixed pair, the bracket at LLL is u(0)‾(−v′(0))−(−u′(0))‾v(0)\overline{u(0)}(-v'(0))-\overline{(-u'(0))}v(0)u(0)​(−v′(0))−(−u′(0))​v(0), which is −u(0)‾v′(0)+u′(0)‾v(0)-\overline{u(0)}v'(0)+\overline{u'(0)}v(0)−u(0)​v′(0)+u′(0)​v(0), the negative of the bracket at 000. The difference across the interval is therefore minus twice the bracket at 000, which is not zero in general. Take u=vu=vu=v with u(0)=1u(0)=1u(0)=1 and u′(0)=iu'(0)=\iiu′(0)=i, which a cubic can arrange along with the two conditions at LLL, and the bracket at 000 is 2i2\ii2i.

(c) The verification in §7.3 treated the two ends separately and used only that the coefficient at each end is real, so it goes through unchanged with ψ′(0)=α0ψ(0)\psi'(0)=\alpha_0\psi(0)ψ′(0)=α0​ψ(0) and ψ′(L)=−αLψ(L)\psi'(L)=-\alpha_L\psi(L)ψ′(L)=−αL​ψ(L) for real α0,αL\alpha_0,\alpha_Lα0​,αL​. That is two of the four, once Dirichlet is counted as the limiting value at each end. The remaining two are the ones that couple the ends to each other, which the periodic and antiperiodic conditions use and the Robin family does not. A Robin condition never lets the wavefunction at one wall know anything about the other.

(d) Self-adjointness is a requirement on an operator, not a description of one, and P2 says every observable is self-adjoint rather than that every self-adjoint operator is the observable you want. The four parameters index four different physical situations, distinguished by their energy levels, and §7.4's table shows three of them disagreeing in the first digit. What decides which one describes a given box is the physics of its walls, and no amount of checking self-adjointness will produce that. The same confusion in Chapter 4.2's language would be reading P2 as a converse, which that chapter's §4.4 explicitly declined to assert.

The brick you just laid — an operator is a formula and a domain, and the domain is forced

The restriction is not a choice. Chapter 0.6 proved that every linear map on Rn\R^{n}Rn is bounded and named the derivative as the operator that breaks the proof in infinite dimensions. Section 2.2 measured the break: on the modes eikx\ee^{\ii kx}eikx the norm stays fixed and the norm of the derivative grows without limit, so momentum is unbounded, which is what an unbounded physical quantity has to look like. Section 2.3 then closed the escape route. A symmetric operator defined on the whole of a Hilbert space is bounded, by the closed graph theorem in two lines, so an unbounded observable cannot be defined on the whole space. The domain of p^\hat pp^​ is compulsory.

And the adjoint gets a domain nobody chose. Chapter 0.5's defining relation for A^†\hat A^{\dagger}A^†, read where A^\hat AA^ acts on a subspace, becomes a test that some vectors pass and others fail, and the set of vectors that pass is dom⁡(A^†)\operatorname{dom}(\hat A^{\dagger})dom(A^†). Density is what makes the answer unique, and it is doing that job and no other. The two domains move in opposite directions: enlarging the operator shrinks its adjoint, so a self-adjoint operator is a place where two moving subspaces meet. Symmetric is the containment. Self-adjoint is the equality. Chapter 4.2's P2 was stated with the finite-dimensional word and now reads self-adjoint, which is the correction that chapter's §4 named this section for.

Three intervals, one operator, three different answers, and all of it integration by parts. Keeping the boundary term of Chapter 0.2 §3.2 rather than dropping it gives iℏ[u‾v]ab\ii\hbar\big[\overline u v\big]_a^{b}iℏ[uv]ab​ as the exact obstruction to symmetry. On R\RR it vanishes by itself, both domains are the same set, and momentum is a unique observable. On [0,L][0,L][0,L] it vanishes exactly when v(L)=eiθv(0)v(L)=\ee^{\ii\theta}v(0)v(L)=eiθv(0) for one fixed phase, giving a circle of momentum operators whose ladders of allowed values slide as the phase turns, and showing that the natural choice of pinning both ends is symmetric and not self-adjoint. On [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) it forces v(0)=0v(0)=0v(0)=0, that domain is not self-adjoint, and nothing larger is symmetric. The momentum of a particle confined to a half-line is not an observable at all, and the argument used nothing beyond ∣v(0)∣2=0\abs{v(0)}^{2}=0∣v(0)∣2=0.

The count, quoted after the answers were already in hand. Von Neumann's classification reduces the question to solving A^†f=±iλf\hat A^{\dagger}f=\pm\ii\lambda fA^†f=±iλf with no boundary conditions and counting square-integrable solutions. For momentum those solutions are e∓p0x/ℏ\ee^{\mp p_0x/\hbar}e∓p0​x/ℏ, and the indices come out (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) on the line, (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) on the interval and (1,0)(1,0)(1,0) on the half-line, matching §5 three times out of three. Placing the mark after the hand calculation rather than before it was deliberate: the theorem is checked against arithmetic you own.

The number this chapter owed, and a correction with it. The same count run on −ℏ2d2dx2/2m-\hbar^{2}\dvn{2}{}{x}/2m−ℏ2dx2d2​/2m over [0,L][0,L][0,L] gives (2,2)(2,2)(2,2), because a second-order equation has a two-dimensional solution space and every solution is square-integrable on a bounded interval. So the particle in a box has a U(2)U(2)U(2) of self-adjoint Hamiltonians: four real parameters, not one. The single parameter belongs to momentum, and carrying it across is the mistake §7 exists to prevent. Dirichlet, Neumann, periodic, antiperiodic and the Robin family are all points of that U(2)U(2)U(2). Solving the Robin slice gives the transcendental condition tan⁡kL=2αk/(k2−α2)\tan kL=2\alpha k/(k^{2}-\alpha^{2})tankL=2αk/(k2−α2), whose roots at α=0\alpha=0α=0 reproduce n2π2ℏ2/2mL2n^{2}\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}/2mL^{2}n2π2ℏ2/2mL2 to every digit printed and at other settings do not, which is the measurement the table and the figure report.

Two marks, and where completeness was spent. The closed graph theorem in §2.3, used once, for Hellinger–Toeplitz and nothing else. Von Neumann's classification in §6.2, quoted with its hypotheses and then checked against three cases already worked. Nothing else here is asserted without being derived, and in particular the whole of §5, which is the section two sentences of Chapter 4.2 point at, uses neither mark. One mark standing elsewhere is leaned on, Fubini's theorem from Chapter 0.2 §4.2, in the grind box of §5.2, cited there rather than re-raised, which is the same treatment Chapter 4.3 gave Heine–Cantor. Chapter 4.3's closing brick said this chapter would need completeness at every step, and the exact answer is that it was spent twice, both times inside one of those two quoted theorems. The closed graph theorem is false on an incomplete space, and von Neumann's carries a Hilbert space in its hypothesis for the same kind of reason. Everything in between runs on two other things Chapter 4.3 supplied, density and Cauchy–Schwarz, and saying which is which is better than crediting the whole chapter with everything.

Where this gets spent. Chapter 4.5 is the third instalment of the bill Chapter 0.5 named, and it needs this chapter's output as its hypothesis: its spectral theorem is stated for self-adjoint operators, which is a condition about domains and nothing else, and its Stone's theorem in §9 is what makes "time evolution is unitary" and "the Hamiltonian is self-adjoint" the same statement. The shape has now repeated twice and it is worth saying in the same words: Chapter 0.4 built the space and Chapter 0.5 built the operators on it. Chapter 4.3 builds the space and Chapters 4.4 and 4.5 build the operators on it. Chapter 4.7 takes §7's U(2)U(2)U(2) and spends one paragraph, not one clause, on why the infinite well selects the Dirichlet point of it. Chapter 4.12 needs the domain language to state honestly that single-valuedness of a wavefunction in the azimuthal angle is an assumption about the domain of L^z\hat L_zL^z​ rather than a theorem. Chapter 4.13 needs §5.5, because the radial coordinate lives on a half-line and the behaviour of the hydrogen wavefunction at the origin has to be argued rather than assumed. What you do not yet have is the values: an operator with no eigenvectors in the space still has a set of possible readings, and naming that set is the whole of Chapter 4.5.
